Guided Inquiry

1 · The free wavepacket

Here’s our particle. A free particle — no forces anywhere — is built here as a wavepacket: plane waves with momenta spread σ around a mean ℏk₀, added with Gaussian weights A(k). The upper plot draws the real and imaginary parts of ψ(x,t), and the lower plot shows the probability density P(x,t) — where the particle can be found. At t = 0, the packet rests as a single hump at x = 0.

2 · A free particle’s width

Let’s start with something familiar. A classical free object — a coasting ball — keeps its sharp position forever, because nothing pushes or pulls it. This quantum packet is just as free. So when time runs, what do you think its width will do?

3 · Why it spreads

So the hump widened and its peak fell. But why does a free packet spread at all? What’s your best explanation?

4 · Give it momentum

Now let’s add some momentum. The packet is rebuilt at t = 0 with mean momentum k₀ = 1. When time runs, what do you expect the probability hump to do?

5 · A narrower packet

Back to rest for this one. The momentum spread is doubled to σ = 2, so the initial hump in x starts twice as narrow. Compared with the σ = 1 packet, how do you think it spreads?

6 · A heavier particle

One last experiment. Keep σ = 2, but make the particle five times heavier: m = 5. Its spread of momenta is unchanged. How do you think the packet spreads now?

About the Simulation
Physics: This simulation follows the Lecture 6 construction: a free-particle wavefunction is built from A(k), evolved with the lecture's α(t), and displayed as Re[\sqrt{C}\psi], Im[\sqrt{C}\psi], and P(x,t).

Visualization: The upper plot shows the real and imaginary parts of \sqrt{C}\psi(x,t). The lower plot shows the lecture probability density P(x,t) = C|\psi|^2. For each slider choice, the vertical axes are fixed from the initial state rather than changing during the time evolution.

Controls: Adjust k₀, σ, and m. Here σ is the lecture's momentum-space width, so smaller σ produces a broader packet in position space.

Note: Here σ is the width in k-space, not the usual position-space Gaussian width. If the packet spreads beyond the visible x-window, the displayed norm drops below 1.
Equations

The Physics

Time evolution of a Gaussian wavepacket · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Nothing pushes a free particle, so it looks like the simplest case in mechanics. This sim builds a Gaussian wave packet from three numbers (k₀, σ and m) and follows it in time, as the wavefunction in the upper plot and as a probability density in the lower.

What you'll learn

  • How a packet is built from plane waves, and what σ measures (it is not a width in x).
  • How to read ψ and the probability density P(x,t) off the two plots.
  • How the packet's centre and width depend on k₀, σ, m and the time t.
  • How large the effect is for an electron, an atom and a grain of dust.
The two plots at t = 0, drawn for k₀ = 2, σ = 1.

What's on screen

  • Upper plot, blue: Re[√Cψ], the real part of the wavefunction.
  • Upper plot, purple: Im[√Cψ], the imaginary part. √C is a constant, so P = (Re)² + (Im)².
  • Lower plot, green: the probability density P(x,t) ≥ 0. Its total area is 1.
  • Live Metrics: Time, xpeak (the centre of P), σ²|α|² (the width readout), Peak P, v = ħk₀/m and Norm (the area under P).
See itSet k₀ = 2, σ = 1, m = 1 and hold the clock at t = 0. Watch for: blue and purple ripples inside the hump of the upper plot, and one smooth green hump below.

Changing k₀, σ or m rebuilds the packet at t = 0. Fixed: ħ = 1, time is in the sim's own "a.u.", and the plots show x from −40 to 40. Each plot's vertical scale is set from the t = 0 state of the current k₀, σ, m, so a shrinking curve means a shrinking value.

03

A packet is a sum of plane waves

A plane wave eikx has momentum ħk and no position. A localised packet adds many of them, with Gaussian weights centred on k₀: A(k) ∝ exp[−(k − k₀)²/2σ²].

Left: the weights A(k). Right: P(x,0), at the opening settings (solid) and at σ = 2 (dashed).
  • σ is the spread in k, not in x. |A|² has standard deviation σ/√2, so Δp = σħ/√2.
  • At t = 0 the sum is a smooth hump times a carrier wave: ψ(x,0) ∝ e−σ²x²/2 · eik₀x. The hump sets the shape of P. k₀ sets the ripples inside it.
  • The hump has width Δx(0) = 1/(σ√2), so a wider A(k) means a narrower hump. Together, Δx(0)·Δp = ħ/2.
See itRaise σ from 1 to 2, with the clock held at t = 0. Watch for: Peak P doubling from 0.5642 to 1.1284 as σ²|α|² falls from 1.000 to 0.250.
04

Every momentum runs its own clock

A free plane wave evolves as ei(kx − ħk²t/2m): its phase turns at the rate ħk²/2m, which depends on k. The packet is the sum, taken with the same weights A(k).

The sim draws the closed form of this integral, with α(t) = 1/σ² + iħt/m.
The lower plot. Only two numbers inside P ever change.
  • xpeak is the centre of the hump. σ²|α|² is the width readout, equal to 2Δx².
  • The prefactor 1/(σ√π|α|) falls as |α| rises, so the hump flattens while its area stays 1. Norm stays 1.00 unless the packet outgrows the ±40 window.
See itRun the packet at k₀ = 0, σ = 1, m = 1. Watch for: σ²|α|² climbing and Peak P falling, while Norm holds at 1.00.
05

The centre moves at ħk₀/m

Left: where the hump is. Right: how wide it is.
  • Drift. The centre moves at v = ħk₀/m, the group velocity. That is the speed of a classical particle with momentum p = ħk₀. A negative k₀ moves it left.
  • k₀ is absent from the width law. A moving packet spreads exactly as a resting one does.
  • Check: with k₀ = 1 and m = 1, v = 1, so xpeak equals the Time readout. With m = 2, xpeak is half of that.
See itRun the packet at k₀ = 1, σ = 1, m = 1. Watch for: xpeak counting up at the same rate as Time, while σ²|α|² climbs as it did at rest.
06

The width grows on the time scale τ

τ is the moment when σ²|α|² has doubled.
k₀ σ m

These sliders move the sim too.

  • τ grows with m and falls with σ². A heavier packet spreads more slowly. A packet that starts narrower in x (larger σ) spreads faster.
  • Since τ = 2m·Δx(0)²/ħ, halving the starting width cuts τ by four.
See itRun σ = 1 and σ = 2 at k₀ = 0 and m = 1, each stopped at Time 2. Watch for: the packet that started narrower ending up wider.
See itRun m = 1 and m = 5 at σ = 2, each stopped at Time 4. Watch for: the two σ²|α|² values differing by a factor of more than 20.
07

Momentum stays fixed, phases do not

A phase factor cannot change a magnitude.
  • Each component keeps its weight |A(k)|, so the momentum spread Δp = σħ/√2 never changes. Only the phases turn.
  • Components with larger k move faster (ħk/m), so they separate. At late times, Δx ≈ Δp·t/m.
  • That sorting shows in ψ. For k₀ = 0 the local wavenumber is k(x) = ħtx/(m|α|²): small at the centre, larger toward the edges. At late times k ≈ mx/ħt.
  • Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2 is a floor. The packet sits on it only at t = 0.
See itRun k₀ = 0, σ = 1, m = 1 and stop at Time 6. Watch for: long, slow ripples near the centre of the upper plot and shorter ones toward its edges.
08

Where it matters

  • Electrons. Localised to 0.1 nm, an electron has τ = 2mΔx(0)²/ħ ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁶ s. A free packet that small would double σ²|α|² in about 0.17 fs.
  • Cold atoms. A ⁸⁷Rb atom localised to 1 µm has τ ≈ 2.7 ms, a laboratory time scale.
  • Everyday objects. A 1 g bead localised to 1 µm has τ ≈ 6 × 10¹¹ years, about forty times the age of the universe. Spreading is real, and unobservable.
Go deeper: the sim in atomic units
τ = 2m·Δx(0)²/ħ for four packets. Log scale: the electron and the bead differ by about 35 orders of magnitude.
  • The sim sets ħ = 1 and gives m in electron masses. It does not name a length unit, only "a.u." for time.
  • If x is in bohr radii and time in atomic units (1 a.u. = 24.19 as), then σ = 1 and m = 1 give Δx(0) = 0.707 bohr ≈ 0.037 nm and τ = 1 a.u. ≈ 24 as.
09

Summary

In one line. A free Gaussian packet's centre moves at v = ħk₀/m like a classical particle, while its width grows from Δx(0) on the time scale τ = m/σ²ħ, with the momentum spread fixed.

Key points

  • The packet is a sum of plane waves with Gaussian weights; σ is the spread in k, and Δx(0)·Δp = ħ/2.
  • xpeak = ħk₀t/m. The width law σ²|α|² = 1/σ² + σ²ħ²t²/m² does not contain k₀.
  • Δx(t) = Δx(0)√(1 + (t/τ)²), with τ = m/σ²ħ = 2mΔx(0)²/ħ.

Common mix-ups

  • "σ is the width of the hump." σ is the spread in k. The hump's width is Δx(0) = 1/(σ√2), so a larger σ gives a narrower hump.
  • "The packet spreads because probability leaks away." The area under P stays 1 (Norm reads 1.00 until the packet outgrows the ±40 window). The peak falls because the same area spreads wider.
  • "Momentum holds a moving packet together." k₀ only moves the centre. The width law has no k₀ in it.

Things to try on your own

  • Set k₀ = 1, σ = 1, m = 1. Predict the Time at which xpeak reaches 3, then check the readout.
  • Set σ = 2, m = 5. Compute τ, then find the Time at which σ²|α|² has doubled from 0.250 to 0.500.
  • Set k₀ = 0, σ = 1, m = 1. Using Δx(t) = Δx(0)√(1 + (t/τ)²), predict when Peak P has halved from 0.5642, then check.
